mathgap.title: Signed difference equality
mathgap.principle: When a statement equates one signed difference to another, translate it directly as (A - B) = (C - D), preserving the order of the names on each side.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a sentence describes a difference equality, e.g., "The number of X that A has more than B is equal to the difference between the number of X that C has and D".
mathgap.example: Interpreting "The number of oranges that Alice has more than Bob is equal to the difference between the number of oranges that Carol and Dave have" as |Alice - Bob| = |Carol - Dave| (absolute differences) instead of (Alice - Bob) = (Carol - Dave).

mathgap.title: Direct count assignment at point of mention
mathgap.principle: When a statement directly gives a count for a person, set that person's current count to the stated value at that point in the narrative; later operations may modify it.
mathgap.when_to_apply: For sentences like "X has N items" that appear in the story.
mathgap.example: Treating "Myles has 15 oranges" as a permanent final count and never updating Myles after later transfers.

mathgap.title: Non‑negative integer check
mathgap.principle: All item counts must be non‑negative integers; any solution that yields a negative or non‑integer count should be discarded as invalid.
mathgap.when_to_apply: After solving equations or applying operations, verify each person's count.
mathgap.example: Accepting a derived count of -3 bananas for a person, which violates the non‑negative integer rule.

mathgap.title: Directionality of more/fewer statements
mathgap.principle: Interpret "X has N more items than Y" as X - Y = N (i.e., X = Y + N) and "X has N fewer items than Y" as X - Y = -N (i.e., X = Y - N).
mathgap.when_to_apply: Whenever a sentence uses the words "more" or "fewer" to compare two quantities.
mathgap.example: Translating "Taylor has 5 fewer oranges than Adolfo" into Taylor - Adolfo = -5, but then using the opposite sign in later equations, which flips the intended relationship.

mathgap.title: Split‑all handling
mathgap.principle: When a person splits all their items equally among two recipients, each recipient receives half of the original count (the total is assumed even), and the original person ends with zero.
mathgap.when_to_apply: For statements like "X splits all the items she owns equally among Y and Z."
mathgap.example: Giving each recipient half of X's items but also leaving X with the same half, instead of setting X's count to zero.

mathgap.title: Targeted constraint extraction for queried variable
mathgap.principle: When the goal is to find a specific person's count, first gather all equations and statements that involve that person, reducing the system to the relevant subset before solving.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Immediately after identifying the target variable, before attempting to solve the full system.
mathgap.example: Attempting to solve the entire network of equations when only a few involve the target person, leading to unnecessary complexity and possible errors.

mathgap.title: Sequential transfer handling with updated counts
mathgap.principle: When a transfer statement appears, immediately subtract the transferred amount from the giver and add it to the receiver, using the current counts at that point.
mathgap.when_to_apply: For sentences like "X gives N items to Y." that occur in the narrative.
mathgap.example: Adding N to the receiver's count but forgetting to subtract N from the giver, resulting in an inflated total.

mathgap.title: Substitution of known signed differences into signed difference equalities
mathgap.principle: If a signed difference on one side of an equality is already known from a direct statement or previous computation, substitute its numeric value into the equation to simplify and solve for unknowns.
mathgap.when_to_apply: When solving a signed‑difference equality where one side has been determined earlier.
mathgap.example: Leaving (Francis - Isabell) as a symbolic term even though Francis = Isabell + 2, instead of replacing it with the known value 2.

mathgap.title: Chronological evaluation of statements
mathgap.principle: Process the statements in the order given, updating counts after each step; later statements refer to the updated counts from earlier operations.
mathgap.when_to_apply: Throughout solving, especially when transfers, conditionals, or difference statements appear after earlier modifications.
mathgap.example: Using a person's initial count in a later "more than" statement even though a prior transfer changed that count.

mathgap.title: Increase‑by‑times handling
mathgap.principle: When a statement says a person's count "increases by N times", interpret it as a multiplicative increase: new count = old count × N.
mathgap.when_to_apply: For sentences like "The number of cucumbers that X has increases by 2 times."
mathgap.example: Interpreting "increases by 2 times" as old + 2 instead of old × 2, which leads to an incorrect final count.

mathgap.description: Treating signed difference statements as absolute differences
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model drops the order of names and assumes differences are always positive, losing sign information.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Keep the order of the names and translate the statement as a signed difference (A - B) = (C - D).

mathgap.description: Ignoring the sequential order of transfers
mathgap.why_it_happens: The model treats all transfers as simultaneous, forgetting that earlier transfers affect later counts.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Apply each transfer in the order presented, updating the giver's and receiver's counts before processing the next statement.

mathgap.description: Assuming explicit counts are final after all transfers
mathgap.why_it_happens: Direct count statements are taken as immutable facts, even when later statements modify those quantities.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Treat a direct count as setting the value at that point in the narrative; allow later transfers or operations to change it.

mathgap.description: Misinterpreting "increase by N times" as addition rather than multiplication
mathgap.why_it_happens: The phrase is ambiguous; the model defaults to an additive reading instead of the intended multiplicative one.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Recognize that "increase by N times" means multiply the current count by N (new = old × N).

mathgap.why_it_happens: The model skips "If X has more than N items, X will transfer..." clauses, treating them as irrelevant.
mathgap.how_to_avoid: Evaluate the condition using the current count; if the condition holds, perform the specified transfer before proceeding.
